newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain's digital TV platform battle heats up.
newsitem.headline: Spain's digital TV platform battle heats up.

text.p: A bitter and complex dogfight over the establishment of a platform for digital television in Spain heated up on Tuesday with yet another name-calling editorial in the worsening crisis.

The battle for control of Spain's underdeveloped pay TV market, which moved into the courts last week, pits the conservative government and one main media group against the leading Socialist opposition and the other main media group.

Tuesday's editorial in pro-conservative newspaper El Mundo criticised pro-Socialist newspaper El Pais for an editorial on Sunday that accused the government of persecuting its parent media group Promotora de Informaciones SA (Prisa).
In an angry front-page editorial on Sunday, El Pais said a court case filed last week against Sogecable, which is 25 percent owned by Prisa and 25 percent owned by France's Canal Plus, was frivolous.

El Mundo responded on Tuesday: "They are more worried about public opinion than about their own court complaint where they know there is little they can do given the clarity of the alleged crime they are charged with."

Sogecable directors are accused of fraud and misappropriation of funds for allegedly misusing customer deposits for pay television. The company filed an appeal on Monday calling the complaint unfounded.
The complaint alleges that Sogecable, which manages Spain's only pay television channel Canal Plus, used 23 billion pesetas ($159 million) of deposits to underwrite a purchase of television decoders.

Both majority owners of Sogecable -- Prisa and Canal Plus -- are partners along with Antena 3 in Spain's first digital television platform CanalSatelite, which has filed a suit against Spain before Europe's Competition Commission.
CanalSatelite accuses the government of abusing its power by introducing regulatory obstacles to favour a rival digital platform that has participation from state-owned companies.

The rival platform is led by recently privatised telecoms operator Telefonica and includes Mexico's Televisa and the state's Radio and Television of Spain (RTVE). It will use state-owned satellite Hispasat.
The government plans to introduce rules to block the sale of CanalSatelite digital television decoders in favour of decoders or unscramblers that could be used for all digital platforms.
The conservative government's Development Minister Rafael Arias-Salgado says the universal decoders were intended to ensure free choice for viewers.

But its key parliamentary ally, the Catalan coalition, has accused the government of interference in the digital platform battle and a related battle for football viewing rights and has said it would not support the proposed regulations.

Part of the digital platform war stems from a move by Antena 3, a commercial station that owns the lucrative rights to televise Spain's most popular football matches, from the Telefonica, favoured by the government, to CanalSatelite.

El Mundo, whose relentless attacks on the former Socialist government helped put the conservatives in power, has published reports accusing Antena 3 chairman Antonio Asensio of moving to CanalSatelite only after failing to get government consessions.
Antena 3 Television fanned the flames on Monday, saying that it had filed suit against El Mundo countering its claim.
